title: Winter, Pollution and Children's Lungs: Why Doctors Want Extra Care This November
excerpt: Children's developing lungs, faster breathing rates and immature immune systems make November's pollution peak especially risky, paediatric specialists say. The warning signs that mean a cough is no longer 'just seasonal' are specific.
body:
• November combines cooler air, still winter conditions and post-Diwali pollution, pushing particulate levels to among the worst of the year — and children are the most exposed group, paediatric specialists say.
  • The mechanism: fine particles such as PM2.5 penetrate deep into developing lungs, irritate airways and weaken their natural defences, aggravating asthma and raising the risk that a respiratory infection becomes pneumonia.
  • The scale in India: pneumonia accounted for 16.3% of deaths among children aged 0-4 in the Sample Registration System estimates for 2021-23, and global estimates put annual under-five pneumonia deaths in India at around 129,000.
  • Act the same day if a child is struggling to breathe, has pauses in breathing, develops bluish lips, becomes unusually sleepy or struggles to feed. Infants under three months with a temperature of 38°C or higher need prompt medical assessment.

Every November, the same combination returns: cooler air, still winter conditions and pollution that settles instead of dispersing. For children's lungs, doctors say, it is the riskiest month of the year — and the danger is that the early signs look like an ordinary seasonal cough.

Why children are hit harder

Children face higher risk for three physical reasons, Dr Amit Gupta, a senior consultant paediatrician and neonatologist at Motherhood Hospitals in Noida, explained in comments reported this month: their lungs are still developing, they breathe faster than adults relative to their size, and their immune systems are not fully mature. Fine particulate matter — PM2.5 and PM10 — along with nitrogen dioxide and ground-level ozone irritates the respiratory tract; in young lungs, those particles travel deep and trigger airway inflammation.

"Children have developing lungs, and their respiratory systems are particularly vulnerable to environmental irritants and infections," said Dr Aditya K. Chawla, Consultant in Interventional Pulmonology at Pacific OneHealth, New Delhi, ahead of World Pneumonia Day on November 12, as reported by Drug Today Online. Pollution does not directly cause every case of pneumonia, doctors note, but it weakens the lungs' defences and makes existing breathing problems worse — which is how a viral cough becomes a hospital visit.

The burden behind the warning is not abstract. India records the world's highest number of pneumonia deaths among children under five. Pneumonia accounted for 16.3% of deaths among children aged 0-4 in the Office of the Registrar General's Sample Registration System estimates for 2021-23, making it the second-leading cause of death in that age group; global estimates released in 2025 by the Forum of International Respiratory Societies put the annual figure at around 129,000 under-five deaths.

The warning signs that change the decision

Dr Nikhil Rajvanshi, Consultant Paediatric Pulmonologist at Rainbow Children's Hospital, Delhi, advises parents to treat specific signs as the line between home care and a doctor, in guidance reported by Health and Me: a cough that persists, recurs at night, or worsens with physical activity should be evaluated rather than dismissed as seasonal, as should recurrent wheezing. A child who is struggling to breathe, has pauses in breathing or develops bluish lips needs emergency care. Dr Chawla adds fast or difficult breathing, unusual sleepiness and difficulty feeding to the list of signs that should not wait.

What parents can do this month

The precautions doctors repeat are unglamorous and specific. Check the AQI before planning outdoor activity, and on high-pollution days move play indoors and skip strenuous outdoor exercise. Keep windows closed during peak pollution periods and use a HEPA air purifier if one is available. Older children who can tolerate one safely should wear a well-fitted N95 — doctors advise against putting masks on babies and young infants. Indoors, avoid smoking, incense sticks, mosquito coils and strong cleaning sprays around children.

Two medication rules matter. Children with asthma should follow their prescribed action plan and use inhalers or nebulisation only as their doctor advised — inhaled medication should not be started or stopped without medical guidance — and parents should not routinely give antibiotics or over-the-counter cough and cold medicines without consulting a paediatrician. Finally, vaccination: doctors stress keeping scheduled doses on time, including the pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV) given under India's Universal Immunisation Programme, which protects against serious pneumococcal infections that can lead to pneumonia. Good nutrition and a smoke-free home do the rest of the protective work.
